name: Lilliane Angella Namala's Path to System Change

content.title: Lilliane Angella Namala's Path to System Change
content.summary: Lilliane's research and policy shift led to confident advocacy and real-world impact

media.caption: Lilliane Angella Namala blends teaching, policy, and advocacy to drive meaningful change in schools in Uganda
media.alt: Lilliane Angella Namala's Path to System Change

content.text: WhenLilliane Angella Namala, a passionate classroom teacher with five years of experience in Uganda, enrolled in theMaster of Education (M.Ed.)in Leadership and Managementpart-time programme at theAga Khan University, Institute for Educational Development, East Africa (IED, EA)in 2021, she was seeking answers. Whyeducational systemsfacing declining performance? Was the solution rooted in leadership, management, or policy?
"I joined IED, EA driven by a thirst for knowledge and a desire to understand the intersection between leadership, management, and educational reform," she reflects.

Liliane initially explored theEarly Childhood elective, but she soon realised that understanding policy was the true key to influencing real change. She transitioned her focus toPolicy Studies in Education. This shift allowed her to critically engage with Uganda's national education policies and strengthen her leadership perspective.

Thepart-time structureof the M.Edprogrammeallowed her to balance work, study, and advocacy. "The programme nurtured my critical thinking, policy analysis, and practical problem-solving skills," she says. She creditsher lecture and supervisor Dr Tage for providing invaluable mentorship that pushed her to apply her learning to real-world contexts, thinking beyond academic boundaries.

One of her most impactful projects involved analyzing the2019 National Teacher Policy in Uganda, which requires all teachers to hold a bachelor's degree. This study inspired her to  launch aYouTube channel,
, dedicated to advancing teacher development and promoting climate education.
"That project showed me that research and advocacy can coexist." she shares. "Learning at AKU inspired me to act."

Throughout her studies, Lilliane applied her enhanced understanding of education policy and evidence-based strategies to both her teaching and advocacy work. In her classroom, she introduced active learning and critical reflection techniques. Meanwhile, her online platform became a vital tool for professional development and climate awareness among teachers and students alike.

Balancing her multiple roles was a challenge, but the programme instilleddiscipline, resilience, and confidence. "It awakened potential beyond academics. AKU taught me to lead, innovate, and influence positive change," she says.

Today, Lilliane continues to use her M.Edlearning to strengthen Uganda's education system through research and advocacy. Her journey proves how the part-time programmeempowers working educators to grow both professionally and personally without stepping away from their calling to serve.

"I encourage all educators and school leaders to pursue the MEd part-time programme," she advises. "It empowers working professionals to think critically, lead confidently, and make meaningful impact in their communities."
